mcqs.question: How does the kernel's generic I/O code invoke a device-specific driver without containing any device-specific logic itself?
options: It recompiles itself for each device at boot time
It only supports one device at a time and never mixes device types
It calls into the driver through a fixed interface (like a table of function pointers), so the generic code stays identical regardless of which driver is behind it
Device-specific logic is written directly into the generic layer for every supported device
mcqs.explanation: The generic layer calls a fixed interface — a standard set of operations every driver implements — without knowing or caring what's on the other side. This is the abstraction that lets one read() implementation work across arbitrarily many device types.

mcqs.question: Why can a hard disk be accessed via lseek() to any position, while a keyboard's input device generally cannot?
options: Disks are block devices with genuinely random-access physical storage; keyboards are character devices producing an ordered stream of events with no addressable positions
Keyboards physically support seeking but the OS disables it for security
It's an arbitrary API restriction with no connection to the hardware
Disks are always character devices, and the block/character distinction only applies to network devices
mcqs.explanation: The block/character distinction reflects genuine physical access patterns: disks store fixed-size, randomly addressable blocks, while a keyboard just emits a sequential stream of keypress events with no concept of a specific offset. The driver interface follows this hardware reality rather than being arbitrary.

mcqs.question: Why does cat /dev/ttyUSB0 (a serial port) look identical at the read() call site to cat file.txt (a regular file), even though the underlying hardware is completely different?
options: Serial ports are internally implemented as regular files on disk
The generic I/O layer dispatches read() through a driver-specific function pointer without needing to know the device type; both drivers implement the same generic interface
cat has special-case code for every device type
read() only works on regular files; the serial port case is actually handled by a completely different syscall
mcqs.explanation: Both devices' drivers implement the same generic read operation; the kernel just follows a function pointer to whichever driver is registered for that file descriptor. cat itself has no device-specific logic — the abstraction lives entirely in the kernel's I/O layer.

mcqs.question: What is the main trade-off of running a device driver in userspace instead of kernel space?
options: Userspace drivers gain full hardware access with no downside at all
Userspace drivers isolate crashes to just that process instead of the whole kernel, at the cost of extra overhead crossing the user/kernel boundary
Userspace drivers cannot be used for any high-performance devices
Userspace drivers eliminate the need for any kernel involvement whatsoever
mcqs.explanation: The core trade-off is fault isolation versus performance: a userspace driver crash doesn't take down the kernel, but crossing the user/kernel boundary more often adds overhead. High-performance frameworks like DPDK do use userspace drivers, and the kernel is still involved in setup even when the data path is userspace-managed.

mcqs.question: Why can a bug in a network card's driver crash the entire kernel, not just break networking?
options: Network drivers are given deliberately unstable code by default
The kernel automatically isolates every driver into its own protected memory space
Kernel-space drivers run at the same privilege level as the rest of the kernel with no memory protection boundary, so corruption can spread beyond the driver's own scope
Only network drivers have this property; other driver types are fully isolated
mcqs.explanation: In a monolithic kernel, all kernel-space code — including every driver — shares the same privilege level and address space, so a bug anywhere can corrupt state anywhere. This applies to any kernel-space driver, not just network drivers, and there's no automatic per-driver isolation in that model.

mcqs.question: Why is ioctl() a more common source of driver bugs and security vulnerabilities than read() or write()?
options: ioctl() is deprecated and no longer used by any modern driver
ioctl() only works on block devices, making it inherently riskier
ioctl()'s arbitrary command-and-argument design means the generic kernel layer can't validate arguments the way it validates read/write sizes, pushing correctness entirely onto each driver
read() and write() are implemented in hardware, so they cannot have bugs
mcqs.explanation: ioctl()'s flexibility — arbitrary command numbers and arguments interpreted however a driver wants — means there's no generic validation the kernel can apply, unlike the well-defined size/offset semantics of read/write. This pushes correctness entirely onto individual drivers, a real and recurring source of bugs and CVEs.
